paragraphs.text: Lesson 30, losing your temper.
Listen to this conversation between Jack and his wife Lynne, who lost her temper at work.
Mark each sentence as true or false as you listen.
Hey, how was work today?
You don't want to know.
I don't have a job anymore.
Are you serious?
What happened?
Well, we were short handed because Todd called in sick, so I was the only server on the floor.
That was fine for a while because the restaurant was totally dead.
And then at like 930 when things in the kitchen are winding down, this whole group of tourists
burst in.
Really?
You guys don't normally get tourists?
We've been getting more lately.
Someone put us in one of those off the beaten path guides.
Ah, so now you get flooded with tourists looking for an authentic place to eat.
Yeah, so anyway, here come all these tourists and I'm running around like a chicken with
its head cut off, trying to get them seated and take their orders.
And they're all pestering me with a million questions about the menu.
I'm just trying to keep my cool.
Where was your boss?
She usually pitches in when the place gets busy, right?
That's the thing.
She was nowhere to be found.
Finally I get all the drinks served and then I go in the back to look for a high chair
and three more booster seats.
Oh no, there were children?
So many children.
I gathered that it was some kind of homeschooling group on a field trip.
Anyway, I'm back there looking around frantically for a booster seat and I hear my boss calling
my name from the office.
Go to the office and I'm like, why?
She starts asking me about my tickets from last night and I told her I couldn't talk
about it because I was swamped with tables.
She just frowned and said to come talk to her about it as soon as I could.
Did she offer to help?
Nope.
So I just dashed back out front and started scribbling down orders.
It wasn't that bad actually.
Everyone was pretty patient because they could see that the place was a madhouse and I was
the only server.
Well, that's good.
I hate it when people can't just chill out and wait.
The customers were nice but the cooks were pretty pissed off when they got all those orders
in the window at once.
Hey, I'd be pretty grouchy too if I had to make 30 entrees at the tail end of my shift.
They were basically throwing the plates at me.
But I got everything served and once the checks were paid the whole place just cleared
out at once.
I figured I'd take a breather before cleaning up so I sat down for a sec.
And that's when my boss finally appears and yells at me because the tables are dirty.
She said I was slacking off.
And that was the last straw.
Uh oh, I'm afraid to ask.
But what did you do?
Took off my apron, threw it at her and stormed out at the place.
Ha, I thought you were home a bit early.
So what now?
Right now I'll just have a drink and veg out in front of the TV a bit.
And tomorrow I'll get cracking on some job applications.
Let's learn the vocabulary from this situation.
When Jeff asks Lynn about her day, she says you don't want to know.
That expression means that the answer will not be pleasant to hear.
Lynn explains that the restaurant was short-handed because a coworker called in sick.
If a place is short-handed, it means it lacks the necessary number of employees because some
people are absent.
For a while, that was fine because the restaurant was totally dead.
The word dead in this context is an informal way to say there were no people and there was
no activity in the restaurant.
But then, around 9.30, things in the kitchen were winding down.
Winding down means getting less active and preparing to finish.
Then, a big group of tourists burst in.
To burst into a place means to come in quickly and suddenly with lots of energy.
Jeff remarks that Lynn's restaurant doesn't usually get tourists, but Lynn says that they've
been getting more tourists lately because the restaurant appeared in one of those off-the-beaten
path guides.
If something is off-the-beaten path, it is away from the main tourist or the main popular
areas, so now the restaurant gets flooded with tourists.
Flooded means filled, possibly with too much or too many of something.
So, when the tourists came in, Lynn was running around like a chicken with its head cut off.
This expression means to move around crazily without direction or organization.
And the tourists were all pestering her with questions about the menu.
To pester somebody means to bother that person persistently.
Lynn was just trying to keep her cool.
To keep your cool means to stay calm and not get angry.
Jeff asks, where was your boss?
She usually pitches in when the place gets busy.
To pitch in means to help, usually to help other people who are already doing the work.
But Lynn says her boss was nowhere to be found.
Lynn went into the back room to look for a high chair and three more booster seats.
A high chair is a raised chair, usually with a platform.
It's designed for a baby to sit in.
And booster seats are plastic seats that are placed on top of a regular chair so that
a small child can reach the table easily.
There were a lot of children in the group of tourists.
Lynn says, I gathered that it was some kind of homeschooling group on a field trip.
I gathered means I figured out from observation.
And a field trip means a trip that is part of an educational experience.
So schools usually take their classes on field trips.
In this case it was a group of homeschooling families, meaning parents who educate their
children at home instead of sending them to school.
So Lynn was in the back room looking around frantically for a booster seat.
Frantically means anxiously and with a sense of urgency.
When her boss called her, she went to the office.
She says, I'm like what?
I'm like is an informal way to say I said.
She couldn't talk to her boss at the moment because she was swamped with tables.
This word swamped means she was overwhelmed.
She had far too much work to do.
Lynn's boss frowned and said to come talk to her as soon as possible.
To frown means to make an upset expression on your face.
You frown when you're sad, angry or when you disapprove of something.
So Lynn dashed back out front and started scribbling down orders.
To dash means to run a short distance.
And to scribble down means to write something on paper very fast and sloppily, not neatly.
Fortunately, the customers were pretty patient because they could see that the place was a
madhouse.
A madhouse is a crazy, chaotic place.
Jeff comments that he hates it when people can't just chill out and wait.
Chill out means relax.
Lynn mentions that the cooks in the kitchen were pretty pissed off when they got a ton
of orders at once.
Pissed off means angry.
Jeff says he'd be grouchy too if he had to make 30 entrees at the tail end of his shift.
Grouchy means in a bad mood.
And the expression the tail end means the final part right at the very end before you finish.
At the tail end of my shift, a shift is a period of work.
We usually use the word shift for people who work hours that are not normal nine to five
hours.
People who work in cafes, hospitals, restaurants, as well as bus drivers might work a shift,
for example, of 4 pm to 10 pm, or of 6 am to 2 pm.
Anyway, Lynn says that after the big group left the restaurant, she figured she'd take
a breather before cleaning up.
To take a breather means to take a quick break just to relax and catch her breath.
So she sat down for a sec.
A sec means a second.
Then, Lynn's boss appeared and yelled at her because the tables were dirty.
She said that Lynn was slacking off.
Slacking off means being lazy and not putting an effort to do the work you're supposed to
be doing.
That, Lynn says, was the last straw.
The last straw is the final thing that makes a situation impossible to tolerate.
Lynn took off her apron, threw it at her boss, and then stormed out of the place.
An apron is a covering for your clothes that is to be used while cooking or serving food.
So Lynn removed her apron and threw it at her boss.
Then she stormed out.
To storm out means to leave a place angrily.
Jeff asks her, so what now?
Tonight, Lynn just wants to have a drink and veg out in front of the TV.
To veg out means to relax in a mindless way.
Then, tomorrow, she says, I'll get cracking on some job applications.
Get cracking is an informal way to say start.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice.
And the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
